title: Rosemary infusion for circulation
subtitle: A warming infusion for sluggish peripheral circulation
excerpt: A simple hot infusion of fresh or dried rosemary leaf, made at 1 teaspoon dried (or 1 teaspoon fresh) per 200 ml cup. Traditionally taken for poor peripheral circulation, cold hands and feet, and mild fatigue. One to two cups a day, for up to four weeks.
sourceNotes: Maud Grieve, A Modern Herbal (1931), Rosemary (Salvia rosmarinus, formerly Rosmarinus officinalis) entry : circulatory-stimulant and tonic uses. King's American Dispensatory (Felter and Lloyd, 1898), Rosmarinus section. Traditional western herbal use of rosemary as a peripheral circulatory stimulant.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Dried leaf stores up to 12 months in a sealed tin. Prepare each cup fresh. Fresh rosemary sprigs from the garden or kitchen work well.

glossaryTerms.definition: A herb traditionally used to encourage peripheral blood flow, associated with warming cold extremities and improving circulation to the hands and feet.

content.text: Rosemary infusion for circulation is a hot-water preparation of Salvia rosmarinus leaf. Fresh sprigs from the garden or dried leaf from a jar both work well. Traditionally taken as a

for poor peripheral circulation: cold hands and feet, a feeling of sluggishness, and the general rundown quality that can accompany winter months. One teaspoon of dried leaf (or one generous sprig of fresh leaf) per 200 ml cup, steeped covered for 5-8 minutes. One to two cups a day.

attrs.title: Precautions
attrs.body:
Not medical advice. Consult a qualified herbalist or doctor for ongoing or serious symptoms.

Rosemary at culinary levels is well tolerated. At the therapeutic dose used in this preparation (one teaspoon of dried leaf, twice daily), consult a herbalist or your midwife before use in pregnancy. The pregnancy caution applies to therapeutic doses; occasional culinary use of rosemary as a kitchen herb is not affected.

Paediatric use is not adult-divided-by-half. Consult a herbalist who specialises in children's herbal medicine before using any herbal preparation in children under twelve.

items.prepNote: dried leaf, or 1 fresh sprig (approx 5 cm)

content.text: Bring fresh cold water to the boil and set aside for one minute.
Place the dried or fresh rosemary in a teapot or a cup with a tea infuser. Pour 200 ml of just-off-boil water over the herb and cover immediately.
Steep covered for 5-8 minutes. The water should pick up a clear, resinous rosemary aroma. Longer steeping increases the bitterness.
Strain into a cup and drink warm.

One to two cups a day. Take for up to four weeks, then take a two-week break before another course. Rosemary is warming and stimulating; taking it in the evening may interfere with sleep in some readers.

Dried rosemary stores for up to 12 months in a sealed tin away from light. Prepare each cup fresh; do not store the prepared infusion. Fresh rosemary sprigs keep a week in a glass of water on the worktop, or up to two weeks wrapped in a damp cloth in the fridge.
When not to use this remedy

See a doctor for persistent fatigue lasting more than a few weeks. Fatigue with weight loss, fatigue with shortness of breath, or fatigue that does not improve with sleep and rest. Anaemia, thyroid disorders, and other treatable conditions cause these symptoms and need assessment.

Cold hands and feet that are accompanied by colour changes in the fingers (white. Blue, red in sequence) on cold exposure may shows Raynaud's phenomenon, which deserves a medical assessment rather than home herbal treatment.
